screens.narratorSegment: When a Linux system becomes slow, the root cause is often a resource bottleneck: the C P U, R A M, or disk. By the end you’ll be able to run a short checklist to locate the bottleneck, identify the offending process or device, and choose the right remediation. Think about a slow server you’ve seen: this chapter will give you the tools to find what’s actually blocking progress.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Diagnosing System Resource Issues
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Diagnosing System Resource Issues

Learn to identify CPU, memory, and disk bottlenecks and act on the correct resource using core Linux tools and safe procedures.

In this lesson
CPU
Use top, htop, and ps to find CPU-hungry processes and identify high user or system usage.
Memory
Inspect available memory, swap, and slab caches with free, vmstat, and slabtop to detect leaks and pressure.
Disk I/O
Measure device utilization and wait times with iostat and diagnose capacity with df and du.
Action
Select the correct remediation — e.g., free memory, tune I/O, or limit CPU usage — based on the diagnosis.
Explore Key Topics
Load Average
Shows how many processes are ready or waiting for I/O over 1, 5, 15 minutes.
Available Memory
The amount the kernel can give to new apps without swapping — don’t confuse it with 'free'.
%util & Await
Key iostat metrics: device busy percentage and average I/O wait time to detect disk saturation.
Visual Concept
Card-based diagnosis path
Observe
Measure CPU, memory, and disk metrics to find the stressed resource.
Confirm
Use device stats and process lists to confirm the specific culprit.
Act
Choose remediation targeted to the bottleneck: tune, restrict, or increase the resource.
Key Takeaway

A clear diagnostic sequence — observe, confirm, act — prevents wasted effort and targets the real bottleneck.

Coming up
We’ll explore CPU tools, memory checks, disk I/O metrics, and a hands-on scenario using the exact commands you'd run on a server.

screens.title: What is a resource bottleneck?
screens.narratorSegment: A resource bottleneck occurs when a system’s performance is limited by one component whose capacity is exceeded by demand. In Linux, the three most common bottlenecks are C P U, memory, and disk input and output. The C P U bottleneck happens when the processor spends most of its time executing user or kernel instructions; you’ll see high user or system percentages. Memory bottlenecks arise when available R A M is low and the system resorts to swap, slowing execution because disk is much slower than R A M. Disk input and output bottlenecks occur when storage is saturated — devices are busy nearly all the time and input and output requests wait, which you can measure as high device utilization and long await times. A frequent misconception is treating a high load average as automatically meaning C P U saturation. Load average counts processes ready to run and processes waiting for input and output, so a high value can also mean heavy disk waiting. A concrete example: a database doing many reads may show low C P U busy but very high input and output wait; adding C P U cores won’t reduce query latency, improving storage throughput will. Key idea: identify which resource is constrained before making changes. How would you check whether a slow service is C P U- or input and output-bound?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › What is a resource bottleneck?
Core Concept

Resource Bottleneck

A resource whose capacity is exceeded, causing system slowdown. Typical culprits: CPU, memory, disk I/O.

CPU
High user or system percentages show intense processor work.
Memory
Low available memory and continuous swap indicate memory pressure.
Disk I/O
High device utilization and long await times show storage saturation.
Concrete example
Imagine a database server with queries waiting. top shows low CPU busy but 'wa' at 50%. iostat reports device %util near 95% and await high. The system is waiting on disk reads. Adding CPU will not help; you must improve storage throughput or change the workload.
Key Takeaway

Measure first. Match the metric to the resource to pick the right fix.

Common misconception
A high load average does not always mean CPU overload; it can reflect many processes waiting for I/O.

screens.title: Using top, htop, and ps to find process issues
screens.narratorSegment: The first tools you reach for are top, htop, and ps because they connect resource numbers to specific processes. top and htop provide a dynamic view of C P U and memory usage and display load averages and C P U state breakdowns like user, system, and input and output wait. htop presents a friendlier, color-coded interface and makes sorting and process selection simpler, while top is available almost everywhere. Use ps for a scriptable snapshot; for example, running a command that sorts by memory lets you quickly list the top consumers. A typical workflow is to watch top to see if C P U or input and output wait is high, then use ps to capture a process snapshot for later analysis. A common mistake is reading only the 'used' memory column in free and concluding memory is exhausted; instead check 'available' and swap usage. Concrete example: if top shows a process consuming 80 percent C P U in the user column, that process is C P U-bound. If top shows low user and system but high input and output wait, the process may be blocked on disk. Practice: open htop, press the sort key to order by C P U, then note the top PID. Use ps aux --sort=-%mem to get a sorted snapshot for memory. Which tool would you use when you need a scriptable one-liner versus a live view?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Using top, htop, and ps
Process Tools

top / htop / ps

Interactive tools show live CPU, memory, and per-process usage. ps provides a snapshot suitable for scripts.

# interactive views
htop
# classic top
top

# snapshot sorted by memory
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 12
Example
If htop shows PID 2345 at 80% CPU, that process is using the CPU heavily. If top shows 'wa' high while CPU usage is low, check disk stats.
Explanation & Tips
  • Use htop to sort processes by CPU or memory and to interactively filter or send signals.
  • ps is scriptable: ps aux --sort=-%mem helps find top memory users for automation or reporting.
  • Don’t assume high load average equals CPU saturation; check 'wa' and the CPU breakdown first.
Key Takeaway

Choose interactive tools for live triage and ps for reproducible snapshots. Match the tool to the task.

screens.title: Reading top: CPU states and load average
screens.narratorSegment: top gives a quick summary of C P U states and the system load average. The C P U breakdown typically lists user time, system time, and input and output wait. User time indicates time spent running user processes; system time reflects kernel operations. input and output wait shows the percentage of time the C P U is idle while waiting for disk operations to complete. Load average is a separate metric that measures how many processes are either runnable or waiting for input and output over the 1, 5, and 15 minute windows. A common misunderstanding is equating load average directly with C P U saturation. For instance, many processes waiting for disk input and output can raise the load average while C P U busyness remains low. A concrete scenario: you see load averages of 8, 7, 6 on a 4-core server, but C P U utilization shows low user and system percentages with 'wa' at 40 percent. This suggests many processes are waiting on disk rather than competing for C P U cycles. The action is to examine disk device metrics with iostat and identify which device has high %util and await. A simple check is to correlate top's wa with iostat's results; if both point to storage, focus on input and output remediation or capacity. What confusion have you seen when looking at load numbers in production?

keyIdea.title: Interpretation rule
keyIdea.text: High load average requires checking CPU usage and I/O wait to determine whether processes are CPU-bound or waiting on I/O.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Reading top: CPU states and load average
Definition

CPU States & Load Average

User and system percentages show CPU work. I/O wait shows idle time spent waiting on disk operations. Load average tallies runnable and I/O-waiting processes over time.

us
Time in user-space execution.
sy
Time in kernel-space (system calls).
wa
Time CPU waits for disk I/O.
Contrast & Guidance
  • High user+system → CPU-bound: consider optimizing code or offloading work.
  • High wa with low CPU busy → I/O-bound: measure device %util and await with iostat.
  • High load average alone → ambiguous; check CPU states and I/O metrics before concluding.
Key Takeaway

Always correlate load average with CPU state breakdown and I/O metrics to find the true bottleneck.

screens.title: Memory basics: free, vmstat, and slabtop
screens.narratorSegment: Memory problems often show up as swapping, slow responsiveness, or application crashes with out-of-memory messages. The free command gives a quick human-readable summary of total, used, free, shared, buffers, cached, and importantly 'available' memory. Focus on 'available' rather than raw 'free' because cached memory can be repurposed by the kernel. vmstat reports virtual memory and system statistics, including swap in and swap out, and shows the C P U input and output wait in the C P U section. Running vmstat with a short interval provides a live sense of trends. For deeper kernel-side memory analysis, slabtop reports kernel slab cache usage and helps detect kernel memory hold-ups that are not visible in user-space. A concrete example: if free shows low available memory and vmstat reports non-zero swap in and swap out counts, the system is under memory pressure and using disk for memory — this will slow workloads. A common mistake is assuming high 'used' memory always indicates a leak; many systems use R A M for caching to speed input and output and this is normal. Verify swap usage and trends over time to differentiate cache usage from real shortage. When would you check slabtop instead of only free and vmstat?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Memory basics: free, vmstat, and slabtop
Tools

free / vmstat / slabtop

Use free for a quick snapshot, vmstat for trending, and slabtop for kernel slab cache investigation.

# snapshot of memory
free -h

# brief live vmstat sample
vmstat 1 5

# kernel slab cache view
slabtop
Explanation
  • Read 'available' in free to know how much the kernel can give to new processes without swapping.
  • vmstat's si and so columns show swap in and swap out; sustained swap means memory pressure.
  • Use slabtop when kernel objects are consuming unexpected memory, indicating a potential kernel-level leak.
Key Takeaway

Distinguish cached memory from true shortage by focusing on available and swap trends, not raw used numbers.

screens.title: Available memory vs cache and swap
screens.narratorSegment: Linux uses free R A M to cache files and speed reads; this is normal and beneficial. The 'available' field in the free command tells you how much memory the kernel can hand to new processes without swapping. Many learners mistake the 'used' column as an indicator of shortage because caches increase 'used' while still leaving ample memory for applications. Swap usage, however, is the clearest sign of memory pressure when it is sustained. If swap is constantly non-zero and growing, the system is relying on disk-based virtual memory and performance will degrade. For example, if free -h shows available at a few hundred megabytes and swap is empty, the system is not necessarily memory-constrained despite high 'used' value. Conversely, if available is low and swap usage is high or increasing, you may have an application leak or need more R A M. Use vmstat to watch si and so columns: repeated swap in and out indicates active swapping. A common misconception is to immediately add R A M when caches are high; instead profile processes with ps or top to find the actual memory consumers before changing hardware. What would you check first: cached memory totals or swap trend?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Available memory vs cache and swap

Available vs Cached

Cached memory accelerates reads and increases 'used'. 'Available' is the meaningful value for whether new apps can run without swapping.

Command
free -h
Check swap
If swap is being used steadily, watch vmstat for si/so to see if swap activity is sustained, indicating memory pressure.
Example & Advice
A server with high cached memory but with hundreds of megabytes available and no swap usage is healthy. If available is low and swap is high, find the process using the most memory and verify whether leaking code or misconfiguration is to blame.
Common Mistake

Don’t equate high 'used' with shortage; inspect 'available' and swap before resizing hardware.

screens.title: Disk I/O with iostat: %util, await, and requests
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output problems often create the most pronounced system slowdown because many applications block while waiting for reads or writes. iostat provides per-device statistics including read/write rates, requests per second, and critical fields: %util and await. Percentage utilization near 100 percent indicates the device is busy nearly all the time. Await is the average time input and output requests take — a high await shows long latencies. For diagnosis, run extended statistics with iostat -xz 1 to see a live feed. When you see %util close to 100 and await rising, you have a disk bottleneck. A practical check is to run a controlled disk load like creating a large temporary file with synchronous writes and observe iostat change. The hands-on chapter suggests using dd to write a large file and watching %util and await for the device. Remember safety: always remove test files when done. A common misconception is to blame the filesystem or application when the underlying device is saturated; iostat helps separate device-level saturation from other causes. After identifying a busy device, consider moving input and output, throttling writers, or upgrading storage throughput. How might you reduce device utilization for a noisy log-heavy service?

keyIdea.title: Disk metric focus
keyIdea.text: Use iostat -xz with live sampling; watch %util for how busy the device is and await for the latency callers experience.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Disk I/O with iostat

iostat -xz 1

Extended device statistics updated every second show read/write throughput, r/s and w/s, await, and %util.

sudo iostat -xz 1
# watch device lines for %util and await
%util
Percentage of time the device was busy; near 100% suggests saturation.
await
Average wait time for I/O requests; rising await means higher latencies for callers.
Example test
In a separate terminal, generate I/O then watch iostat. Example shown in the hands-on activity uses dd to write a large file and then removes it when finished.
dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile.img bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync
rm tempfile.img
Key Takeaway

High %util and high await together indicate device-level bottleneck. Confirm with a controlled I/O test and then plan remediation.

screens.title: Storage capacity: df and du for safe cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: Capacity problems are distinct from performance but often cause real issues when a partition fills. df -h shows mounted filesystem usage and helps you find partitions that are nearing full. Once you know which mount is full, du -sh on suspect directories reveals which folders consume the most space. A practical pattern is to run df to locate the full mount, then run du on likely application directories such as /var/log or application data paths. Be extremely careful when deleting files — the rm -rf command is permanent and can remove critical data if used on the wrong path. Consider archiving or moving files rather than immediate deletion, and verify paths twice. For example, if df -h reports /var at 95 percent, du -sh /var/log can show whether logs are the largest contributor. If logs are huge, compress or rotate them rather than bluntly deleting important recent logs. This step may resolve apparent slowness caused by lack of free space as services fail to write or behave unpredictably when disks are full. What safe steps would you follow before removing files from a critical mount?

This step may resolve apparent slowness caused by lack of free space as services fail to write or behave unpredictably when disks are full. What safe steps would you follow before removing files from a critical mount?

keyIdea.title: Capacity checklist
keyIdea.text: Use df to find full filesystems and du to locate large directories; always verify before deleting and prefer archiving or rotation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Storage capacity: df and du

df -h / du -sh

Locate full filesystems with df and find large directories with du before any deletion.

df -h

# Check directory sizes
du -sh /var/log
du -sh /path/to/app/data
Safety and strategy
  • Verify mount points and paths before issuing deletion commands.
  • Prefer log rotation and archiving to permanent deletion; compress and move files to another storage when possible.
  • Use checksums or listings if you need to ensure content before removal.
Warning

When using rm -rf, double-check the path. Mistakes here can permanently destroy critical data.

screens.title: Hands-on scenario: diagnosing a slow system
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario follows a clear sequence: observe, confirm, and act. Start by observing the system with an interactive tool like htop to see C P U meters, process lists, and load averages. If you spot high C P U percentages, sort by C P U to find the offending PID. If load averages are high but C P U busy is low and input and output wait is significant, open a second terminal to run iostat -xz 1 and watch device metrics. To evaluate memory pressure, run free -h and vmstat with a short sampling window to watch swap in and out counts. The lab also includes a controlled disk test using dd to generate input and output and observe how %util and await change; do this in a separate terminal and delete the temporary file afterwards. A concrete step sequence from the chapter: run htop, run free -h and vmstat 1 5, install sysstat if needed and run iostat -xz 1, then in another terminal run dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile. img bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync and monitor the device. Finally, use df -h and du -sh on directories like /var/log to check capacity. Common mistakes include running tests on production volumes without cleanup or misreading cache as used memory. Reflect: which single metric would make you focus on storage instead of C P U?

keyIdea.text: Follow a measured sequence: observe live metrics, confirm device or process-level facts, then act with targeted fixes and safe cleanup.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Hands-on scenario
Step-by-step
  1. Open htop and observe CPU bars, load average, and process list; sort by CPU if needed.
  2. Run free -h and vmstat 1 5 to check available memory and swap activity.
  3. Install sysstat if missing and run sudo iostat -xz 1 to monitor device %util and await.
  4. In a separate terminal, generate disk I/O using dd to confirm device saturation, then remove the test file.
  5. Use df -h to find full partitions and du -sh on large directories before cleaning up files safely.
Commands (copyable)
htop
free -h
vmstat 1 5
sudo apt install sysstat   # or the package manager for your distro
sudo iostat -xz 1
# in another terminal to generate IO
dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile.img bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync
rm tempfile.img

# disk capacity checks
df -h
du -sh /var/log
Key Takeaway

Run a focused sequence, validate the metrics across tools, then take the least disruptive remediation first.

screens.title: Interpreting vmstat: si, so, and wa
screens.narratorSegment: vmstat is a concise way to watch virtual memory and system activity over time. The columns si and so show swap in and swap out counts. When you see repeated non-zero values in si and so, it means pages are moving between disk and memory and the system is spending time on swapping. The C P U section also reports wa, which is the percentage of time the C P U is waiting for input and output. Watching vmstat at a one-second interval helps you see trends: a single spike may not indicate persistent pressure, but sustained non-zero swap or rising wa suggests a systemic issue. For example, run vmstat 1 and observe whether si or so appear repeatedly; if they do while load is high, investigate which process is causing page faults by using ps to list memory consumption. Also correlate vmstat’s wa with iostat’s await: if both show high values, storage is the likely bottleneck. A common mistake is to rely on a single snapshot; use short, repeated samplings to confirm a pattern. After confirming, plan targeted remediation such as reducing working set size, increasing R A M, or improving storage performance. Which vmstat columns would you use to confirm swapping is the primary problem?

keyIdea.text: Use vmstat samples to detect persistent swap activity and I/O wait; sustained si/so values indicate swapping and degraded performance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Interpreting vmstat: si, so, and wa

vmstat sampling

Run vmstat with a short interval to detect sustained swap or I/O waiting that single snapshots can miss.

vmstat 1 10  # sample every second for 10 seconds
# Watch columns: si so (swap in/out), wa (I/O wait)
How to read
  • si/so non-zero repeatedly → system is swapping; investigate memory consumers.
  • wa rising → CPU is idle waiting for I/O; check device metrics with iostat.
  • Use ps or top to map swapping or waits to specific processes.
Common Mistake

Do not react to a single sampled spike. Confirm persistent trends before planning changes.

screens.title: ps and scripting: find the top memory and CPU consumers
screens.narratorSegment: ps is the go-to command when you need a reproducible snapshot suitable for automation or for taking evidence when working with others. Use ps aux --sort=-%mem to list processes by memory consumption or ps aux --sort=-%C P U to list by C P U. These one-line snapshots are easy to capture, store, and share. When diagnosing out-of-memory crashes, a scriptable ps listing helps you correlate which processes were present before the crash. Pair ps snapshots with periodic logging or cron to collect historical evidence. A concrete example: when a process consumes steadily increasing memory, schedule a short ps snapshot every minute and examine the trend. Remember that ps shows a point-in-time view; combine it with vmstat or iostat sampling to correlate resource trends. A common misconception is to rely solely on interactive tools when command-line snapshots are easier to include in incident reports. Practice capturing ps outputs and saving them with timestamps for later analysis. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › ps and scripting

ps snapshots for reporting

ps lets you create reproducible process lists for incidents and automation.

# top memory consumers
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 12

# top CPU consumers
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -n 12

# sample every minute for 10 minutes
for i in {1..10}; do date >> /tmp/ps-sample.log; ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 12 >> /tmp/ps-sample.log; sleep 60; done
Example
Use the sampling loop to capture trends that reveal leaks rather than spikes.
Advice
Combine ps snapshots with vmstat or iostat sampling that covers the same time window to correlate process behavior and resource metrics.

screens.title: Troubleshooting checklist and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When diagnosing system slowness, follow a reproducible checklist: observe metrics, confirm with device or process diagnostics, and act with the least disruptive remedy. Start with an interactive observation using top or htop to see C P U, memory, and load averages. If indicators point to memory pressure, check free and vmstat for available memory and swap trends; use ps to find heavy processes. If indicators point to disk issues, run iostat to inspect device %util and await, and use df and du to check capacity. A final tip: prioritize diagnosing the resource shown by multiple tools rather than relying on one measurement. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Troubleshooting checklist

Checklist

  1. Observe: run htop/top, note load averages, CPU breakdown, and any obvious process spikes.
  2. Confirm memory: run free -h and vmstat samples to check available memory and swap trends.
  3. Confirm disk: run sudo iostat -xz 1 to inspect %util and await; use df and du for capacity issues.
  4. Map to process: use ps snapshots to identify the exact process consuming the resource.
  5. Act safely: prefer throttling or configuration changes, archive before deletion, and clean up test files after I/O tests.
Common mistakes
  • Assuming high load = CPU bottleneck.
  • Deleting files without verification.
  • Reacting to single-sample spikes rather than trends.
Pro tip
Collect short, repeated samples from multiple tools to correlate events before changing resources or configuration.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These concise concept cards summarize the key technical definitions you’ll use during diagnosis. C P U utilization measures how much time the processor actively executes instructions and helps decide when a process is C P U-bound. Load average reports the average number of runnable or input and output-waiting processes and must be interpreted together with C P U and input and output wait percentages to avoid false conclusions. A memory leak is a programming bug where an application fails to release memory, causing available memory to fall over time and possibly leading to swap usage. Each concept is tightly connected to a diagnostic action: check C P U percentages and process lists for C P U utilization, and pair load averages with iostat and top to find whether waiting is due to input and output. For memory leaks, use repeated ps snapshots and vmstat samples to detect growth over time. Keep these terms in mind as you practice the hands-on steps; they are the lens through which you interpret what the tools show.

CPU Utilization
Percent of time CPU executes instructions — indicates processor load.
Load Average

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: These additional quick references tie metrics to actions. Swap space is disk-based virtual memory used when R A M is exhausted; heavy swap usage tends to slow the system and signals memory pressure. Disk input and output is composed of read and write operations; when a device's %util approaches 100 and await is high, latency increases for all dependent processes. input and output wait, reported as 'wa', is the C P U state for time spent idle waiting on storage; a high wa tells you to examine storage, not the processor. Use these concepts as decision points: heavy swap or repeated si/so in vmstat → focus on memory; high %util and await in iostat → focus on storage; high user/system C P U percentages → focus on C P U processes. These definitions are practical shortcuts so you can decide which tool to run next and whether the remediation should focus on configuration, code fixes, or hardware changes.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Swap Space
Disk area used as virtual memory when RAM is exhausted; much slower than physical RAM.
Disk I/O
Operations reading and writing to storage; performance measured with throughput, %util, and await.
I/O Wait (wa)
Percentage of CPU idle time spent waiting for disk I/O; a high value points to storage bottlenecks.
Summary Action Map

Swap issues → memory checks; high %util/await → storage checks; high user/system → CPU/process checks. Use tools to confirm before acting.

fullNarratorScript:
When a Linux system becomes slow, the root cause is often a resource bottleneck: the C P U, R A M, or disk. In this lesson we’ll build a repeatable approach so you can determine which resource is overloaded before making changes. You will see how to use interactive tools to view live process activity, snapshot commands to script checks, and device statistics to detect disk saturation. For example, if the C P U is mostly waiting for input and output, adding R A M won’t help — you need to investigate the storage layer. We’ll also practice safety rules for disk cleanup and show how to interpret key metrics like 'available' memory, input and output wait, and device %util. By the end you’ll be able to run a short checklist to locate the bottleneck, identify the offending process or device, and choose the right remediation. Think about a slow server you’ve seen: this chapter will give you the tools to find what’s actually blocking progress.

In this chapter you will gain practical diagnostic skills for C P U, memory, and disk performance. First, you will learn to recognize the common symptoms of each bottleneck: high C P U percentages for processor-bound tasks, low available memory and heavy swapping for memory pressure, and high device utilization and long wait times for disk input and output issues. Second, you will become comfortable using interactive and snapshot tools to observe processes and device behavior. These objectives matter because diagnosing correctly avoids wasted work, such as adding R A M when the disk is the real problem. For example, spotting a high input and output wait percentage means you should measure device %util and await, not immediately increase C P U cores. The Bloom-style progression encourages you to learn tool names, understand their outputs, and apply them in real troubleshooting, moving toward mastery where you can quickly pinpoint and remediate the bottleneck. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can confirm your practical skills.

These objectives are practical: you should be able to run commands and interpret specific fields to reach a diagnosis. For C P U problems, notice user and system percentages and whether the C P U is spending time waiting for input and output; this tells you whether processing or storage is the bottleneck. For memory, learn to read 'available' memory and watch swap usage — persistent swap is a red flag for memory pressure. For disk input and output, interpret iostat's %util and await: a device near 100 percent util with high await suggests the storage is saturated. The final objective ties the tools together: use process listings to map a resource spike to a process or service. A common misconception is treating high load averages as pure C P U demand — always check C P U and input and output wait before deciding. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or mini-visual so you can recall the right next command in real incidents.

A resource bottleneck occurs when a system’s performance is limited by one component whose capacity is exceeded by demand. In Linux, the three most common bottlenecks are C P U, memory, and disk input and output. The C P U bottleneck happens when the processor spends most of its time executing user or kernel instructions; you’ll see high user or system percentages. Memory bottlenecks arise when available R A M is low and the system resorts to swap, slowing execution because disk is much slower than R A M. Disk input and output bottlenecks occur when storage is saturated — devices are busy nearly all the time and input and output requests wait, which you can measure as high device utilization and long await times. A frequent misconception is treating a high load average as automatically meaning C P U saturation. Load average counts processes ready to run and processes waiting for input and output, so a high value can also mean heavy disk waiting. A concrete example: a database doing many reads may show low C P U busy but very high input and output wait; adding C P U cores won’t reduce query latency, improving storage throughput will. Key idea: identify which resource is constrained before making changes. How would you check whether a slow service is C P U- or input and output-bound?

The first tools you reach for are top, htop, and ps because they connect resource numbers to specific processes. top and htop provide a dynamic view of C P U and memory usage and display load averages and C P U state breakdowns like user, system, and input and output wait. htop presents a friendlier, color-coded interface and makes sorting and process selection simpler, while top is available almost everywhere. Use ps for a scriptable snapshot; for example, running a command that sorts by memory lets you quickly list the top consumers. A typical workflow is to watch top to see if C P U or input and output wait is high, then use ps to capture a process snapshot for later analysis. A common mistake is reading only the 'used' memory column in free and concluding memory is exhausted; instead check 'available' and swap usage. Concrete example: if top shows a process consuming 80 percent C P U in the user column, that process is C P U-bound. If top shows low user and system but high input and output wait, the process may be blocked on disk. Practice: open htop, press the sort key to order by C P U, then note the top PID. Use ps aux --sort=-%mem to get a sorted snapshot for memory. Which tool would you use when you need a scriptable one-liner versus a live view?

top gives a quick summary of C P U states and the system load average. The C P U breakdown typically lists user time, system time, and input and output wait. User time indicates time spent running user processes; system time reflects kernel operations. input and output wait shows the percentage of time the C P U is idle while waiting for disk operations to complete. Load average is a separate metric that measures how many processes are either runnable or waiting for input and output over the 1, 5, and 15 minute windows. A common misunderstanding is equating load average directly with C P U saturation. For instance, many processes waiting for disk input and output can raise the load average while C P U busyness remains low. A concrete scenario: you see load averages of 8, 7, 6 on a 4-core server, but C P U utilization shows low user and system percentages with 'wa' at 40 percent. This suggests many processes are waiting on disk rather than competing for C P U cycles. The action is to examine disk device metrics with iostat and identify which device has high %util and await. A simple check is to correlate top's wa with iostat's results; if both point to storage, focus on input and output remediation or capacity. What confusion have you seen when looking at load numbers in production?

Memory problems often show up as swapping, slow responsiveness, or application crashes with out-of-memory messages. The free command gives a quick human-readable summary of total, used, free, shared, buffers, cached, and importantly 'available' memory. Focus on 'available' rather than raw 'free' because cached memory can be repurposed by the kernel. vmstat reports virtual memory and system statistics, including swap in and swap out, and shows the C P U input and output wait in the C P U section. Running vmstat with a short interval provides a live sense of trends. For deeper kernel-side memory analysis, slabtop reports kernel slab cache usage and helps detect kernel memory hold-ups that are not visible in user-space. A concrete example: if free shows low available memory and vmstat reports non-zero swap in and swap out counts, the system is under memory pressure and using disk for memory — this will slow workloads. A common mistake is assuming high 'used' memory always indicates a leak; many systems use R A M for caching to speed input and output and this is normal. Verify swap usage and trends over time to differentiate cache usage from real shortage. When would you check slabtop instead of only free and vmstat?

Linux uses free R A M to cache files and speed reads; this is normal and beneficial. The 'available' field in the free command tells you how much memory the kernel can hand to new processes without swapping. Many learners mistake the 'used' column as an indicator of shortage because caches increase 'used' while still leaving ample memory for applications. Swap usage, however, is the clearest sign of memory pressure when it is sustained. If swap is constantly non-zero and growing, the system is relying on disk-based virtual memory and performance will degrade. For example, if free -h shows available at a few hundred megabytes and swap is empty, the system is not necessarily memory-constrained despite high 'used' value. Conversely, if available is low and swap usage is high or increasing, you may have an application leak or need more R A M. Use vmstat to watch si and so columns: repeated swap in and out indicates active swapping. A common misconception is to immediately add R A M when caches are high; instead profile processes with ps or top to find the actual memory consumers before changing hardware. What would you check first: cached memory totals or swap trend?

Disk input and output problems often create the most pronounced system slowdown because many applications block while waiting for reads or writes. iostat provides per-device statistics including read/write rates, requests per second, and critical fields: %util and await. Percentage utilization near 100 percent indicates the device is busy nearly all the time. Await is the average time input and output requests take — a high await shows long latencies. For diagnosis, run extended statistics with iostat -xz 1 to see a live feed. When you see %util close to 100 and await rising, you have a disk bottleneck. A practical check is to run a controlled disk load like creating a large temporary file with synchronous writes and observe iostat change. The hands-on chapter suggests using dd to write a large file and watching %util and await for the device. Remember safety: always remove test files when done. A common misconception is to blame the filesystem or application when the underlying device is saturated; iostat helps separate device-level saturation from other causes. After identifying a busy device, consider moving input and output, throttling writers, or upgrading storage throughput. How might you reduce device utilization for a noisy log-heavy service?

Capacity problems are distinct from performance but often cause real issues when a partition fills. df -h shows mounted filesystem usage and helps you find partitions that are nearing full. Once you know which mount is full, du -sh on suspect directories reveals which folders consume the most space. A practical pattern is to run df to locate the full mount, then run du on likely application directories such as /var/log or application data paths. Be extremely careful when deleting files — the rm -rf command is permanent and can remove critical data if used on the wrong path. Consider archiving or moving files rather than immediate deletion, and verify paths twice. For example, if df -h reports /var at 95 percent, du -sh /var/log can show whether logs are the largest contributor. If logs are huge, compress or rotate them rather than bluntly deleting important recent logs. This step may resolve apparent slowness caused by lack of free space as services fail to write or behave unpredictably when disks are full. What safe steps would you follow before removing files from a critical mount?

vmstat is a concise way to watch virtual memory and system activity over time. The columns si and so show swap in and swap out counts. When you see repeated non-zero values in si and so, it means pages are moving between disk and memory and the system is spending time on swapping. The C P U section also reports wa, which is the percentage of time the C P U is waiting for input and output. Watching vmstat at a one-second interval helps you see trends: a single spike may not indicate persistent pressure, but sustained non-zero swap or rising wa suggests a systemic issue. For example, run vmstat 1 and observe whether si or so appear repeatedly; if they do while load is high, investigate which process is causing page faults by using ps to list memory consumption. Also correlate vmstat’s wa with iostat’s await: if both show high values, storage is the likely bottleneck. A common mistake is to rely on a single snapshot; use short, repeated samplings to confirm a pattern. ps is the go-to command when you need a reproducible snapshot suitable for automation or for taking evidence when working with others. Use ps aux --sort=-%mem to list processes by memory consumption or ps aux --sort=-%C P U to list by C P U. These one-line snapshots are easy to capture, store, and share. When diagnosing out-of-memory crashes, a scriptable ps listing helps you correlate which processes were present before the crash. Pair ps snapshots with periodic logging or cron to collect historical evidence. A concrete example: when a process consumes steadily increasing memory, schedule a short ps snapshot every minute and examine the trend. Remember that ps shows a point-in-time view; combine it with vmstat or iostat sampling to correlate resource trends. When diagnosing system slowness, follow a reproducible checklist: observe metrics, confirm with device or process diagnostics, and act with the least disruptive remedy. Start with an interactive observation using top or htop to see C P U, memory, and load averages. If indicators point to memory pressure, check free and vmstat for available memory and swap trends; use ps to find heavy processes. If indicators point to disk issues, run iostat to inspect device %util and await, and use df and du to check capacity. Throughout, avoid common mistakes: don’t react to a single snapshot, don’t confuse cached memory with a shortage, and never delete files without verification. For disk tests, perform them on non-production or test volumes when possible and always clean up temporary files. When scripting snapshots, include timestamps and collect multiple metrics to correlate events. These concise concept cards summarize the key technical definitions you’ll use during diagnosis. C P U utilization measures how much time the processor actively executes instructions and helps decide when a process is C P U-bound. Load average reports the average number of runnable or input and output-waiting processes and must be interpreted together with C P U and input and output wait percentages to avoid false conclusions. A memory leak is a programming bug where an application fails to release memory, causing available memory to fall over time and possibly leading to swap usage. Each concept is tightly connected to a diagnostic action: check C P U percentages and process lists for C P U utilization, and pair load averages with iostat and top to find whether waiting is due to input and output. For memory leaks, use repeated ps snapshots and vmstat samples to detect growth over time. Keep these terms in mind as you practice the hands-on steps; they are the lens through which you interpret what the tools show.

These additional quick references tie metrics to actions. Swap space is disk-based virtual memory used when R A M is exhausted; heavy swap usage tends to slow the system and signals memory pressure. Disk input and output is composed of read and write operations; when a device's %util approaches 100 and await is high, latency increases for all dependent processes. input and output wait, reported as 'wa', is the C P U state for time spent idle waiting on storage; a high wa tells you to examine storage, not the processor. Use these concepts as decision points: heavy swap or repeated si/so in vmstat → focus on memory; high %util and await in iostat → focus on storage; high user/system C P U percentages → focus on C P U processes. These definitions are practical shortcuts so you can decide which tool to run next and whether the remediation should focus on configuration, code fixes, or hardware changes.
